A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same privacy-amplification framework and applications. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including v2's added Appendix B.

before.justification: Section 4 and Table 1 report original ResNet-101 private fine-tuning experiments on CIFAR-10, including validation accuracies for different privacy-accounting approaches.

after.justification: Tables 1–2 and Section 4.2 report original centralized and federated fine-tuning results, plus training experiments comparing Balanced Iteration Subsampling with Poisson subsampling.

M1.justification: Random submodel assignment, clipping, Gaussian noise, dropout with probability 0.5, and fixed-participation Balanced Iteration Subsampling remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 are rewritten as clearer pseudocode. The added experiments apply the existing framework without introducing a new proposed component or accounting method.

E1.justification: Coverage expands beyond the original private fine-tuning experiment to simulated federated fine-tuning with user-level privacy and private training from scratch. Sections 4.1–4.2 therefore test additional training and deployment scenarios, although all training evaluations remain on CIFAR-10.

E2.justification: The matched model-splitting comparisons retain standard accounting and the full-model 'relaxation' comparator. Poisson subsampling remains the comparator for Balanced Iteration Subsampling, and the existing RDP/PLD comparison is retained. The new experiments extend these comparisons without introducing another comparator method.

E3.justification: New protocols include federated training with two samples per user, 250 sessions and three local iterations, and WideResNet-40-4 training for 2000 iterations with 655 participations per sample. Parameter sweeps add further budgets and subsampling rates. The retained delta-versus-iterations plot also changes its stated epsilon from 8 in v1 Figure 3 to 10 in v2 Figure 4; this does not establish recomputation.

E4.justification: Figure 1 and Appendix B substantially expand numerical sensitivity analyses of the privacy bounds across submodel counts, iteration budgets, privacy budgets, and sampling rates. Figures 2 and 7–8 examine when the subsampling advantage becomes negligible at larger iteration counts. Figure 7(a) repeats Figure 2 and is not additional evidence.

E5.justification: v1 gives no seed counts or uncertainty summaries for Table 1. v2 identifies Tables 1–2 as best-of-three-seed results with standard deviations around 0.7%, and Section 4.2 also reports best-of-three selection. This newly discloses reporting practices; it does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports federated results, including 80.28% versus 78.47% for amplification versus baseline with three submodels. Section 4.2 adds balanced-versus-Poisson accuracies of 70.21% versus 70.13% from scratch and 84.86% versus 84.99% for fine-tuning. Table 1's accuracies are unchanged, while its noise entries use newly stated normalization. Additional privacy-bound curves expand the numerical evidence.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.4 adds an explicit deterministic-splitting assumption to its statement, with probabilistic mixtures still covered by Theorem 3.5. The principal bounds and all Appendix A proofs remain unchanged. The rewritten Poisson-subsampling formula in Theorem 3.11 is algebraically equivalent.

C1.justification: The abstract changes the Balanced Iteration Subsampling claim from 'stronger' to 'similar or stronger' amplification than Poisson sampling. The introduction emphasizes equitable participation and practical suitability rather than superior privacy alone. The unified framework and model-parallelism contributions remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a practical rationale involving participation fairness and system-load stability, and interprets the nearly equal training outcomes as supporting balanced subsampling when Poisson sampling is unsuitable. The existing explanations of small-versus-large iteration regimes and model-splitting accuracy tradeoffs largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 specifies that table noise values are normalized by expected batch size or number of users, explicitly identifies the baseline as standard RDP accounting for DP-SGD, and names the Sherlock computing cluster. These improve documentation without providing a new implementation release or detailed hardware specification.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to He et al. (2016), Mironov et al. (2019), and Rényi (1961), explicitly asserts novelty for amplification through model parallelism, and integrates the already cited Feldman and Shenfeld work into Remark 3.9. The broader research positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The introduction and explanatory passages receive localized rewrites, and both algorithms receive cleaner pseudocode. Section 4 gains model-splitting and subsampling subsections; acknowledgments, an impact statement, and Appendix B are added. The main narrative sequence and proof organization remain stable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a two-curve iteration/noise plot to a multiple-submodel privacy/noise comparison. v2 adds a federated-results table and extensive multipanel appendix figures, with expanded captions and revised table displays. Matching avoids counting retained v1 Figure 2, now v2 Figure 3, as new content.

improvement.justification: v2 adds direct training evidence for federated model splitting and Balanced Iteration Subsampling, and its more cautious abstract better matches the near-equal Poisson comparisons. Broader sensitivity checks and seed disclosures make the evidence easier to assess. These are useful but bounded gains: the central theory and original accuracies remain unchanged, and best-of-three results with approximate standard deviations still provide limited uncertainty information.
